blocks.p: The deep drawer at the bottom of Higuchi's case was the one closed door in Rei's whole month that had not locked itself. So it was the one he trusted least, and the one he put off longest.

He went back to the Crooked Shelf after closing on a night when the borrowed grain was still faint in his palms. The shop was dark except for a single lamp. Higuchi was asleep on the cot in the back room with a book open on his chest, the way he slept most nights, among the books. Rei did not wake him. He knelt in front of the case, fitted the old dark key into the drawer, and opened it the way a man lifts a dressing he has been afraid to look under.
There was no grimoire. There was no spellbook, no contract that smelled of sulphur, none of the furniture the films had promised for a moment like this.

blocks.cap: The ledger from the deep drawer, read by lamplight

blocks.p: There was a ledger. A plain accountant's ledger, the kind his father had kept, ruled in faint blue. The early pages were in an old, cramped hand, the dead exorcist's. Names had been entered there decades ago and crossed out and entered again as the years went by. The later pages were in Higuchi's careful script. Across the top of the newest page, in a hand so careful it must have taken the writer an hour, was one word.
Registry.
Under it, numbered one to thirteen, were the only thirteen names that mattered in the city Rei had lived in his whole life without knowing they were there.

doc.title: Registry. Current page, in Higuchi's hand
lines: I. Grief. The weight of permanent loss. Asakura Mio. Kyoto. Stable.
II. Rage. The force of perceived injustice. Mori Takao. Tokyo, hard to find. Under pressure.
III. Love. The binding between people. Sakuma Kei. Tokyo. Stable.
IV. Fear. The anticipation of harm. Nakashima Yuna. Tokyo. Under pressure.
V. Wonder. The aperture that opens when something beautiful exists. Chen Lian. Tokyo, the Grid Archive. Stable.
VI. Despair. The collapse of hope. Watanabe Jun. Variable (pencilled beside it. Itabashi, the municipal library, attempting retirement again). Weakening. (starred twice)
VII. Joy. The completion of something good. Hoshino Haru. Kita, Sakae Street. Stable.
VIII. Shame. The internal wound of failing what you cared about. Kobayashi Emi. Tokyo. Stable.
IX. Hunger. The drive toward what is not yet. Inoue Satoru. No fixed location. Under pressure.
X. Courage. The movement forward despite fear. Okabe Natsumi. Independent. Stable.
XI. Longing. The ache for what is absent or gone. Park Junho. Shin-Ōkubo. Under pressure.
XII. Awe. The dissolution of self before something greater. Kasumi Shin. Variable. Stable.
XIII. Duty. The will to persist beyond any single moment. Vacant since 2009. Kita district. Critical, membrane thinning.

blocks.p: He read it the way people read the worst test results, top to bottom, refusing to skip ahead.

They were not gods. That was the first thing the page taught him, and it landed like cold water. The thirteen were not gods and never had been. They were offices. The ledger called them domains, the way a ward has a registrar and a precinct has a captain. Thirteen standing arrangements between the living city and the pressure on the other side of its wall. Each one was an emotion. Each one had a holder. Each one was a discipline that a single person had agreed to carry so that the rest of Tokyo did not have to feel the full weight of it.

Despair had an office. Rage had an office. Fear, Hunger, Longing. Each had a number, a chair and a person. Somewhere in this city those people were alive right now, each bearing one of the thirteen ways the other side leans on the world, so that for everyone else it stayed a mood instead of a flood.
Then there was the thirteenth line. It was different, and Rei knew it would be before his eye reached it, the way a body knows which stair is the broken one in the dark.
Twelve of the lines had names. The thirteenth had only a number and a word, Duty, and beside it, in the same careful hand but pressed harder, almost through the paper, the words vacant since 2009.
No name. No holder. No discipline carried. An office of the city had stood open for six years. There was a chair at the table of the thirteen with no one in it.

Rei sat back on the bookshop floor and understood, finally and completely, what his brother had been pulled toward all month. Not a throne. Not a power. A vacancy. The one unbearable thing the registry had been built never to allow. An office of the wall left unmanned, and leaning.

Higuchi had not only listed the thirteen. He had explained them, in a long note that ran sideways up the margin of the page. The writing got smaller and more frightened the higher it climbed. Rei turned the ledger on its side and read the only honest account of the wall he had ever been given.
A held domain is a chair that leans into the room.

The holder takes the pressure of one emotion onto a single living soul and turns it inward, toward the city. That way Despair stays a private weather inside one person instead of a public flood across a ward. The cost is paid, but it is paid by someone. When people feel any of these thirteen things strongly enough, all at once, the feeling presses on the membrane. The holder takes that pressure and keeps the emotion moving, keeps it in circulation, so that it never settles and pools into the stuff suffering beings are made from.
That is the arrangement. That is the whole secret.

The city stood because thirteen people, most of whom Rei had walked past without a glance, were at this moment holding a door shut with their entire lives. They lived ordinary lives. They had jobs and apartments and habits. The CVD knew only that the old Accord mentioned some kind of stabilising structure. Higuchi had underlined one sentence twice. No one outside a very small group knows the anchors are thirteen people eating breakfast.
A vacant domain, the note went on, is a chair that leans the other way.
Here the hand began to shake. Rei could see it. The blue ink caught and pooled.

With no holder to turn the pressure inward, the office does not close. It cannot close. The registry has no way to retire a seat. Thirteen is a number the wall requires, not a committee that can be made smaller. So the pressure of the thirteenth emotion, with no living person to bear it, leans outward instead. It leans against the seam nearest the empty chair. The membrane there thins. Entity activity rises. And the city feels a wrongness that civilians cannot name.

The seam nearest the empty chair was the one over the district where the chair had last been filled. The last holder of Duty had died in 2009, in Kita. When a holder crosses, the succession is meant to find the next holder by itself, among whoever is near with the right kind of opening to the Font. That night no one with the right aperture was anywhere near. The succession did not take. Since then the thing at the centre that Rei had already met, the one the old books called the Axis, had been carrying the thirteenth seat itself, directly, from inside. Higuchi had written beside that, in letters barely a millimetre tall, not sustainable.
That was why Kita had been coming apart since 2009. That was why March 2011 had torn it so much faster. A vacant office had been pressing its full weight on a single ward for six years.
That is why the dead come so close there at Obon, the note said. And that is why a healer who wished to thin the wall would not need to break it. He would only need to help.
Rei sat with that in the lamplight until the shape of it stopped being information and became the floor of his stomach.

The Healer was not thinning Kita's wall against the grain of the world. It was thinning it along the grain. It was finishing a tear the empty chair had spent six years starting. Every favour, every haunting closed, every grief gently put to rest, had not been the Healer fighting the registry. It had been the registry's own vacant thirteenth seat doing exactly what an empty office does, with a patient demon standing beside it lending a shoulder.

Now he understood why no grade in the city could point to a crime. There had been no crime. There had been a death in 2009, and no one in the right place, and a wall that had been sagging ever since. Everything after that had only been the wall finishing the fall it began before Rei was grown. His brother's hands were the latest, gentlest, most loving thing leaning on a door that had wanted to open since the year the lights went out.
From the back room came the creak of the cot. Higuchi was awake, standing in the doorway in his cardigan, looking at the ledger on the floor and at the boy sitting beside it.
"I told you it would make it worse," he said.
"Did Gin read this?"

"Your brother read it the first winter he came in." Higuchi lowered himself onto a stool with the care of a man whose knees had opinions. "He copied the names into that book of his. Then he stopped coming in. I think he went looking for them."
Rei looked at the starred line. Watanabe Jun. Despair. Weakening.
"Then so will I," he said.
